title: The Return of the Urban Beekeeper

questions.q: Urban honey is now sold for a profit.
questions.evidence: urban honey has become a small but profitable industry
questions.explanation: Paragraph A says urban honey has become **a small but profitable industry**, so the statement agrees with the passage.

questions.q: The number of hives in London grew quickly throughout the 1990s.
questions.evidence: the number of hives only rose sharply after 2008
questions.explanation: Bees were kept in the 1990s, but numbers **only rose sharply after 2008**. The word "only" contradicts rapid growth in the 1990s, so the answer is FALSE.

questions.q: Temperatures in cities are a little higher than in the nearby countryside.
questions.evidence: Cities are also slightly warmer than the surrounding countryside
questions.explanation: "A little higher" paraphrases **slightly warmer**, and "nearby countryside" paraphrases **surrounding countryside**. The answer is TRUE.

questions.q: Research has proved that urban bee colonies are calmer than rural ones.
questions.evidence: there is little scientific evidence to support this claim
questions.explanation: Beekeepers *report* that urban colonies are calmer, but the passage says there is **little scientific evidence** for this. The statement says it has been proved, so it is FALSE.

questions.q: Honey from city hives tastes different from countryside honey.
questions.evidence: slightly less honey than those in the countryside
questions.explanation: Paragraph C compares the **amount** of honey, not its taste. Taste is never mentioned, so the answer is NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: honeybees compete with wild pollinators for the same flowers
questions.explanation: Paragraph C explains that honeybees **compete** with wild pollinators and that some districts have **more hives than the available flowers could support**. That is heading iii.

questions.q: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: several cities have introduced rules for new beekeepers
questions.explanation: The whole paragraph is about **registration, limits and training** for beginners, which matches heading iv.

questions.q: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: Other groups are focusing on food rather than hives
questions.explanation: Paragraph E is about **planting flowers** for insects rather than adding hives. Heading iii is a trap: shortage of flowers is the problem in C, but E describes the solution.

questions.q: Paragraph F
questions.evidence: profit is not the main motivation
questions.explanation: Paragraph F says **profit is not the main motivation** and describes how hives are used to teach pupils. Heading i is a trap: business is mentioned in A, not F.

questions.q: Some London boroughs limit the number of colonies on a single ______.
questions.evidence: limit the number of colonies allowed on a single building
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says some boroughs limit colonies **on a single building**.

questions.q: Poorly managed colonies are more likely to spread ______ to neighbouring hives.
questions.evidence: more likely to spread disease to neighbouring hives
questions.explanation: The rules protect bees because badly managed colonies may spread **disease**.

questions.q: The Berlin scheme chose shrubs that flower in ______, when food is scarcest.
questions.evidence: choosing species that bloom in late summer
questions.explanation: "Flower" paraphrases **bloom**; the answer is **late summer** (two words, within the limit).

questions.q: Wild flowers now grow because councils cut the grass on roadside ______ less often.
questions.evidence: stopped cutting the grass on roadside verges so often
questions.explanation: The word after "roadside" in paragraph E is **verges**.

title: Messages Under the Pavement: The Pneumatic Post

questions.q: an explanation of why early attempts to carry people by air pressure were unsuccessful
questions.evidence: it proved impossible to keep the long leather seals along the track airtight
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says passenger schemes failed because the **leather seals could not be kept airtight**.

questions.q: a description of how workers found a canister that had become stuck
questions.evidence: calculate its position by measuring the air pressure
questions.explanation: Paragraph F explains that workers located blockages by **measuring the air pressure**.

questions.q: a comparison with a more recent form of communication
questions.evidence: compared this to the text messages of the early twenty-first century
questions.explanation: Paragraph E compares pneumatic letter cards to **text messages**.

questions.q: examples of organisations that still use the technology today
questions.evidence: Hospitals, banks and supermarkets continue to use smaller pneumatic systems
questions.explanation: Paragraph G lists **hospitals, banks and supermarkets** as current users.

questions.q: The first working message tube connected two places in the same city.
questions.evidence: linking the stock exchange with the central telegraph station a few hundred metres away
questions.explanation: The London line linked two buildings **a few hundred metres away** from each other, so they were in the same city. TRUE.

questions.q: Delivering a telegram inside a city could take longer than sending it between cities.
questions.evidence: this final stage often took longer than the transmission itself
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says the hand delivery stage **often took longer than the transmission itself**. TRUE.

questions.q: In most networks, canisters could travel in either direction through the same tube.
questions.evidence: canisters travelling in one direction only
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says canisters travelled **in one direction only**, which contradicts the statement. FALSE.

questions.q: Canisters in the tubes moved faster than trains.
questions.evidence: slower than a train but considerably faster than any vehicle in the crowded streets above
questions.explanation: Canisters were **slower than a train**; they were only faster than street traffic. FALSE.

questions.q: The Paris network was longer than the Berlin network.
questions.evidence: the Paris system alone contained more than 400 kilometres of tubing
questions.explanation: The passage gives the length of the **Paris** system only. Berlin's size is never stated, so we cannot compare them: NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: According to paragraph C, tubes were especially valuable in financial districts because
questions.evidence: a delay of ten minutes could cost a trader a fortune
questions.explanation: A **ten-minute delay could cost a trader a fortune**, so speed mattered most there. The other options are not mentioned.

questions.q: The writer says that the cheap letter cards encouraged people to
questions.evidence: they encouraged a brief, almost conversational style of writing
questions.explanation: "Short, informal" paraphrases **brief, almost conversational**. Diaries are mentioned only as historical sources.

questions.q: What were the main reasons for the decline of the pneumatic post?
questions.evidence: The spread of the private telephone after the Second World War removed much of the demand for fast short messages
questions.explanation: Paragraph F names **the private telephone** and the **rising cost of maintaining ageing pipes**. It also says the decline was **gradual rather than sudden**, which rules out A.

questions.q: Why does the writer mention proposals to deliver parcels through underground pipes?
questions.evidence: essentially a larger version of an idea that the nineteenth century had already made work
questions.explanation: The writer presents parcel pipes as **a larger version** of the nineteenth-century idea, showing that it remains relevant.

title: The Elastic Hour: How the Mind Builds Time

questions.q: Paragraph B
questions.evidence: The internal-clock model has proved remarkably durable
questions.explanation: Paragraph B first explains why the clock model has **lasted** (it is testable) and then why it **cannot account for** everyday distortions. Heading vii is a trap: the paragraph says there is **no** convincing evidence of a timing organ.

questions.q: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: A crucial distinction, now widely accepted, is between prospective and retrospective judgements of time
questions.explanation: Paragraph C defines **prospective** and **retrospective** judgements, the two ways of judging duration.

questions.q: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: This distinction helps to resolve what is sometimes called the holiday paradox
questions.explanation: A holiday feels short while it happens but long in memory: the **holiday paradox** in heading iii.

questions.q: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: the brain responds less vigorously to stimuli it has already encountered and can predict
questions.explanation: The oddball effect links **predictable** stimuli to shorter perceived durations, which is heading iv.

questions.q: Paragraph F
questions.evidence: Such findings have prompted a reinterpretation of the familiar complaint that life accelerates with age
questions.explanation: Paragraph F offers a **new explanation** (fewer new experiences) for the feeling that life speeds up with age.

questions.q: Paragraph G
questions.evidence: might lengthen one's life, not in objective terms but in the way it is remembered
questions.explanation: Paragraph G suggests novelty could make life **seem longer in memory**, which matches heading vi.

questions.q: One reason the internal-clock model has survived is that it can be tested experimentally.
questions.evidence: not least because it makes clear predictions that can be tested in the laboratory
questions.explanation: The writer says the model has been durable **not least because** its predictions **can be tested in the laboratory**. YES.

questions.q: Most researchers still dispute the distinction between prospective and retrospective judgements.
questions.evidence: A crucial distinction, now widely accepted
questions.explanation: The writer describes the distinction as **now widely accepted**, which contradicts the statement. NO.

questions.q: A general slowing of biological processes is the most convincing explanation for time seeming to speed up with age.
questions.evidence: there is little experimental support for the idea
questions.explanation: The writer says there is **little experimental support** for this and calls a different explanation **more persuasive**. NO.

questions.q: The oddball effect is stronger in children than in adults.
questions.evidence: they consistently judge the unexpected image to have been displayed for longer
questions.explanation: Paragraph E describes the oddball effect but never compares **age groups**. NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: According to paragraph C, retrospective estimates of time depend mainly on
questions.evidence: the quantity of distinct memories an interval has left behind
questions.explanation: Retrospective estimates depend on **the quantity of distinct memories**. Option A describes *prospective* estimates, which depend on attention.

questions.q: What does the writer say about the suggestion that novelty could lengthen life?
questions.evidence: The claim remains largely untested
questions.explanation: The writer states that **the claim remains largely untested**. "Only half in jest" means it was *partly* serious, so B is wrong.

questions.q: In the oddball effect, the brain's weaker response to predictable images is misread as a ______.
questions.evidence: this reduced response is misread as a shorter duration
questions.explanation: "Weaker response" paraphrases **reduced response**, which is misread as **a shorter duration**.

questions.q: Critics warn that ______ can itself become routine.
questions.evidence: critics caution that novelty can itself become routine
questions.explanation: "Warn" paraphrases **caution**; the word is **novelty**.

title: School Streets: Reclaiming the Road at the School Gate

questions.q: Cyclists are allowed to enter a school street while it is closed.
questions.evidence: only pedestrians and cyclists may enter
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says **only pedestrians and cyclists may enter** during the closure. TRUE.

questions.q: People who live on a school street cannot drive to their homes during a closure.
questions.evidence: Residents who live on the street, as well as emergency vehicles and drivers with disabilities, are normally allowed through
questions.explanation: Residents are **normally allowed through**, which contradicts the statement. FALSE.

questions.q: The first school streets were introduced in Britain.
questions.evidence: The first schemes appeared in northern Italy
questions.explanation: The first schemes appeared in **northern Italy**, not Britain. FALSE.

questions.q: Children breathe more quickly than adults.
questions.evidence: they breathe faster than adults
questions.explanation: "More quickly" paraphrases **faster**. TRUE.

questions.q: Cameras are more effective than volunteers at enforcing closures.
questions.evidence: cameras record the number plates of vehicles that enter without permission
questions.explanation: Both methods are described, but the passage never says which works **better**. NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: The evaluation of thirty-seven schemes also recorded a fall in noise levels.
questions.evidence: levels of nitrogen dioxide, a gas produced mainly by diesel engines, fell by up to 23 per cent
questions.explanation: The evaluation reports **nitrogen dioxide** and travel habits. **Noise** is not mentioned. NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: an example of a scheme that was stopped
questions.evidence: was abandoned after a month of complaints
questions.explanation: Paragraph F describes a trial that **was abandoned after a month of complaints**.

questions.q: a reason why nearby roads may not become as busy as expected
questions.evidence: some families change their habits altogether rather than parking a little further away
questions.explanation: Paragraph E explains that extra traffic is **smaller than feared** because some families **change their habits altogether**.

questions.q: a reference to money that helped councils create more schemes
questions.evidence: local authorities were given emergency funding
questions.explanation: Paragraph C mentions **emergency funding** during the pandemic.

questions.q: a mention of closures becoming permanent
questions.evidence: have become permanent pedestrian areas
questions.explanation: Paragraph G says some closures **have become permanent pedestrian areas**.

questions.q: Nitrogen dioxide is a gas that comes mainly from ______.
questions.evidence: a gas produced mainly by diesel engines
questions.explanation: "Comes mainly from" paraphrases **produced mainly by**: the answer is **diesel engines**.

questions.q: The number of children who were driven to school fell by around a ______.
questions.evidence: the number who were driven fell by around a fifth
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says the number driven **fell by around a fifth**.

questions.q: Schemes are much harder to introduce on main roads or ______.
questions.evidence: much harder to introduce outside schools on main roads or bus routes
questions.explanation: Paragraph F lists **main roads or bus routes** as difficult locations.

title: Chrononutrition: Does the Clock on the Plate Matter?

questions.q: Paragraph B
questions.evidence: almost every tissue in the body contains its own biological clock
questions.explanation: Paragraph B describes the **master clock** and the **peripheral clocks** in body tissues.

questions.q: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: Some of the strongest evidence comes from studies of shift workers
questions.explanation: Paragraph C is built around evidence from **shift workers** and night work.

questions.q: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: the same meal produces a noticeably larger rise in blood sugar when eaten in the evening than in the morning
questions.explanation: Paragraph D explains why **the same meal** affects blood sugar differently in the morning and evening.

questions.q: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: limits all food intake to a window of eight to ten hours each day
questions.explanation: Paragraph E is about **time-restricted eating**, limiting food to an eight-to-ten-hour window.

questions.q: Paragraph F
questions.evidence: the enthusiasm surrounding chrononutrition deserves some caution
questions.explanation: Paragraph F lists weaknesses: **small studies**, **individual variation** and practical difficulty. Heading viii is a trap: diet books appear in G, not F.

questions.q: Surveys of shift workers show that night work causes diabetes.
questions.evidence: Such observational studies cannot prove cause and effect
questions.explanation: The writer says such studies **cannot prove cause and effect**, so the claim that they *show* causation contradicts the writer. NO.

questions.q: Advice that people are unable to follow is not very useful.
questions.evidence: advice that people cannot follow is of limited value
questions.explanation: "Not very useful" paraphrases **of limited value**. YES.

questions.q: Night owls should eat their largest meal late in the evening.
questions.evidence: a schedule that suits a so-called morning lark may not suit a night owl
questions.explanation: The writer says schedules may differ for night owls but gives **no advice** about when they should eat. NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Some diet books make claims that go beyond the current evidence.
questions.evidence: What chrononutrition does not yet justify is the confident, one-size-fits-all rules promoted by some diet books
questions.explanation: The writer says the evidence **does not yet justify** the rules in some diet books. YES.

questions.q: The master clock in the brain is set largely by exposure to ______.
questions.evidence: set largely by exposure to daylight
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says the master clock is **set largely by exposure to daylight**.

questions.q: Insulin sensitivity is highest ______ in the day.
questions.evidence: insulin sensitivity is highest early in the day
questions.explanation: The word is **early**: sensitivity is highest early and declines towards evening.

questions.q: Mice fed a high-fat diet within a restricted window stayed considerably ______.
questions.evidence: remained considerably leaner
questions.explanation: "Stayed" paraphrases **remained**; the answer is **leaner**.

questions.q: A person's natural tendency to be active early or late in the day is called their ______.
questions.evidence: People differ in their chronotype, their natural tendency to be active early or late in the day
questions.explanation: Paragraph F defines **chronotype** as this natural tendency.

title: The Shop That Came to the Door

questions.q: Mobile shops were at their most numerous in the late 1950s.
questions.evidence: At their peak in the late 1950s
questions.explanation: Paragraph A says mobile shops reached their **peak in the late 1950s**. "Most numerous" is a paraphrase of "peak", so the answer is TRUE.

questions.q: The first mobile shops were mainly operated by chemists.
questions.evidence: often run by bakers or grocers
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says the earliest carts were **run by bakers or grocers**. Chemists appear only in paragraph D, as a place drivers collected prescriptions from, so the statement is FALSE.

questions.q: Shopkeepers were able to buy former military lorries at low prices after the First World War.
questions.evidence: thousands of ex-army lorries were sold off cheaply
questions.explanation: "Ex-army lorries were **sold off cheaply**" matches "former military lorries at low prices", so the answer is TRUE.

questions.q: Walter Heslop employed an assistant to help him on his rounds.
questions.evidence: Records kept by one Cumbrian operator, Walter Heslop
questions.explanation: Paragraph C gives Heslop's **mileage, customers and credit sales**, but says nothing about staff. The information is simply not in the passage, so the answer is NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Most of Heslop's sales were made on credit.
questions.evidence: almost a third of his sales were made on credit
questions.explanation: The ledgers show **almost a third** of sales were on credit. A third is not "most", so the passage contradicts the statement: FALSE.

questions.q: a reason why some operators could not meet new legal requirements
questions.evidence: investments that many small businesses could not justify
questions.explanation: Paragraph E explains that hygiene rules demanded **refrigeration and running water**, which many small businesses **could not justify** paying for.

questions.q: a description of how the inside of a vehicle was equipped
questions.evidence: fitted these vehicles with wooden shelves, a counter at the rear
questions.explanation: Paragraph B describes the **shelves, rear counter and paraffin stove** fitted inside the converted lorries.

questions.q: a reference to financial help given to older customers
questions.evidence: cashing cheques for pensioners
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says some operators acted as **informal bankers**, cashing cheques for pensioners. Don't confuse this with credit sales in C, which were for all families.

questions.q: a place where people can view preserved vehicles today
questions.evidence: a small collection of restored vans can now be seen at a transport museum
questions.explanation: Paragraph G mentions **restored vans** on display at a **transport museum** in County Durham.

questions.q: Modern community-owned vans sell groceries and also offer services such as parcel collection and ______.
questions.evidence: services such as parcel collection and library loans
questions.explanation: Paragraph F lists **parcel collection and library loans** as the extra services.

questions.q: Online ordering allows customers to request particular products ______.
questions.evidence: allowing customers to request specific products in advance
questions.explanation: Customers can request specific products **in advance** using online ordering.

questions.q: Supporters claim the vans reduce the number of individual ______.
questions.evidence: reduce the number of individual car journeys
questions.explanation: The passage says the vans **reduce the number of individual car journeys**. "Individual" is already in the sentence, so two words are enough.

questions.q: Critics note that most schemes still rely on ______ rather than sales.
questions.evidence: most of these schemes still depend on public grants
questions.explanation: "Rely on" paraphrases **depend on**; the schemes depend on **public grants**.

questions.q: Paragraph B
questions.evidence: some researchers began to describe it as a resource
questions.explanation: Paragraph B describes a shift from seeing language mixing as **a sign of weakness** to seeing it as **a resource**. Heading viii is a trap: Welsh schools are mentioned only as the origin of a term.

questions.q: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: Pupils in the flexible classes scored, on average, 12 per cent higher
questions.explanation: Paragraph C reports the **test results** of Oduya's study comparing flexible and English-only lessons.

questions.q: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: the difference between understanding a concept and expressing it
questions.explanation: Paragraph D explains that pupils first **grasp the concept** in their best language and only then attach English terms.

questions.q: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: There is also a practical difficulty
questions.explanation: Paragraph E opens with **"Not everyone is persuaded"** and then gives criticisms and a **practical difficulty**.

questions.q: Paragraph F
questions.evidence: it works best as a planned strategy
questions.explanation: The key idea of paragraph F is that translanguaging must be a **planned strategy**, not informal tolerance.

questions.q: Paragraph G
questions.evidence: implications that go beyond language teaching
questions.explanation: Paragraph G moves beyond the classroom to **teacher training, assessment and parents** — wider consequences for schools and families.

questions.q: According to paragraph A, teachers who used pupils' home language were traditionally seen as
questions.evidence: teachers who slipped into the pupils' home language were often regarded as having failed
questions.explanation: Paragraph A says such teachers were **regarded as having failed**. The other options are not stated.

questions.q: The term 'translanguaging' was originally used to describe
questions.evidence: originally used to describe a bilingual teaching method in Welsh schools
questions.explanation: The word **originally** signals the answer: a **bilingual teaching method in Welsh schools**. Its broader meaning (option B) came later.

questions.q: What did Oduya's study find about pupils in the flexible classes?
questions.evidence: their written English was no weaker than that of the control group
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says their written English was **no weaker** than the control group's, and sometimes their technical vocabulary was **more precise**. Options A and C contradict this.

questions.q: The port city study lasted for three years.
questions.evidence: carried out over three years in eleven secondary schools
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says the investigation was **carried out over three years**, so the answer is TRUE.

questions.q: In the rural district study, clear rules about language use led to a fall in pupils' exposure to English.
questions.evidence: without clear rules about when each language should be used, pupils' exposure to English fell by almost half
questions.explanation: The fall happened **without** clear rules, not because of them. The statement reverses the cause, so it is FALSE.

questions.q: In the classrooms Oduya's team observed, pupils' final written work had to be in English.
questions.evidence: required the final written product to be in English
questions.explanation: Teachers **required the final written product to be in English**, which matches the statement: TRUE.

questions.q: The bilingual glossaries were later published for use in other schools.
questions.evidence: Some schools also produced bilingual glossaries
questions.explanation: Paragraph F says the glossaries were **compiled partly by pupils**, but nothing about publication or use elsewhere. The answer is NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: an example of how unlearning could be used dishonestly
questions.evidence: to conceal evidence of biased training data
questions.explanation: Paragraph F warns that unlearning could be used **to conceal evidence of biased training data** — a dishonest purpose.

questions.q: a comparison between the cost of retraining and household energy use
questions.evidence: the annual electricity consumption of 1,200 households
questions.explanation: Paragraph B compares retraining energy with the **annual electricity consumption of 1,200 households**.

questions.q: a reference to organisations changing how they document training data
questions.evidence: keep detailed records of which data was used to train which model
questions.explanation: Paragraph G says some organisations now **keep detailed records** of which data trained which model.

questions.q: an explanation of why removing a record from a database is not enough
questions.evidence: Deleting the original record from a database leaves the model's learned behaviour untouched
questions.explanation: Paragraph A explains that deleting the record **leaves the model's learned behaviour untouched**.

questions.q: Retraining a model from scratch is the most dependable way of removing the influence of data.
questions.evidence: The most reliable approach is also the most obvious
questions.explanation: "Most dependable" paraphrases **most reliable**, and the approach described is retraining from scratch: TRUE.

questions.q: Sharded training produces models that are more accurate than a single model trained on all the data.
questions.evidence: tend to perform less well than a single model trained on all the data at once
questions.explanation: Sharded models **perform less well**, and accuracy falls further as shards increase. The statement says the opposite: FALSE.

questions.q: Approximate unlearning methods can often be completed in a matter of minutes.
questions.evidence: often requiring only minutes of computation
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says approximate methods are fast, **often requiring only minutes**: TRUE.

questions.q: The researchers in paragraph D were employed by a commercial technology company.
questions.evidence: a team of researchers found that models which appeared to have forgotten
questions.explanation: The passage describes only **a team of researchers** and never says who employed them. The answer is NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: Independent logs recording the use of unlearning are already in widespread use.
questions.evidence: no such system yet exists on a large scale
questions.explanation: Such logs have only been **proposed**; **no such system yet exists on a large scale**. The statement is contradicted: FALSE.

questions.q: What did the experiments described in paragraph D show?
questions.evidence: could be prompted to recall them after a small amount of further training on unrelated material
questions.explanation: Models that **appeared to have forgotten** examples could **recall them** after further training. This is why verification is hard.

questions.q: According to paragraph E, legal scholars disagree about
questions.evidence: Some legal scholars argue that the law should require only that the model no longer reveals the individual's data
questions.explanation: One group says the model need only **no longer reveal** the data; the other says **any residual influence** is still processing. The disagreement is about what counts as compliance.

questions.q: In a trained model, information from the data is spread across billions of numerical ______.
questions.evidence: dispersed across billions of numerical parameters
questions.explanation: "Spread" paraphrases **dispersed**; the information is dispersed across numerical **parameters**.

questions.q: In sharded training, a smaller ______ is trained on each portion of the data.
questions.evidence: training a smaller sub-model on each
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says a smaller **sub-model** is trained on each portion. A hyphenated word counts as one word.

questions.q: Data protection laws were drafted with conventional ______ in mind.
questions.evidence: drafted with conventional databases in mind
questions.explanation: The laws were written with **conventional databases** in mind, not statistical models.

title: Echoes in Stone: The Science of Archaeoacoustics

questions.q: Paragraph B
questions.evidence: The basic techniques are borrowed from architectural acoustics
questions.explanation: Paragraph B explains the **techniques borrowed from architectural acoustics** — loudspeakers, microphones and reverberation time. Heading vii is a trap: equipment is mentioned, but not its cost.

questions.q: Paragraph C
questions.evidence: within the lower register of the adult male voice
questions.explanation: Paragraph C describes underground chambers that **resonate** at frequencies of the **adult male voice**.

questions.q: Paragraph D
questions.evidence: Demonstrating that a resonance exists is therefore very different from demonstrating that it was intended
questions.explanation: Paragraph D asks whether resonances were **intended** or simply **a consequence of dimensions** — accident or intention.

questions.q: Paragraph E
questions.evidence: measured echo strength at 64 painted rock shelters and at 58 unpainted shelters
questions.explanation: The comparative study in paragraph E contrasts **painted** (marked) and **unpainted** (unmarked) shelters.

questions.q: Paragraph G
questions.evidence: the field has had a noticeable effect on museum and heritage practice
questions.explanation: Paragraph G describes the field's **effect on museum and heritage practice**, such as demonstrations and conservation plans.

questions.q: Sound was once thought to be impossible to study scientifically in archaeology.
questions.evidence: it was assumed to lie beyond the reach of scientific study
questions.explanation: The writer says sound was **assumed to lie beyond the reach of scientific study** for most of the discipline's history: YES.

questions.q: Digital reconstructions of damaged structures can be relied on to give accurate results.
questions.evidence: the reliability of such reconstructions depends heavily on assumptions
questions.explanation: The writer stresses that reliability **depends heavily on assumptions** about missing features, so they cannot simply be relied on: NO.

questions.q: Finding a resonance in a chamber is sufficient evidence that it was designed deliberately.
questions.evidence: Demonstrating that a resonance exists is therefore very different from demonstrating that it was intended
questions.explanation: The writer says showing a resonance exists is **very different** from showing it was intended. The statement contradicts this: NO.

questions.q: Archaeoacoustics is a more valuable approach than conventional excavation.
questions.evidence: may reveal aspects of past experience that conventional methods overlook
questions.explanation: The writer says the field **may reveal** things other methods overlook, but never ranks it as **more valuable** than excavation. NOT GIVEN.

questions.q: What was measured in the study in southern Africa?
questions.evidence: measured echo strength at 64 painted rock shelters and at 58 unpainted shelters nearby
questions.explanation: The study **measured echo strength** at painted and unpainted shelters. Visibility and water (C) were suggested factors, not measurements.

questions.q: Why have some archaeoacousticians begun working with anthropologists?
questions.evidence: to widen the range of possible interpretations that archaeologists consider
questions.explanation: Paragraph F says the aim is **not to project modern beliefs onto the past** (so A is wrong) but **to widen the range of possible interpretations**.

questions.q: Reverberation time is the period needed for a sound to fade by sixty ______.
questions.evidence: the period taken for a sound to fade by sixty decibels
questions.explanation: Paragraph B defines reverberation time as the time for a sound **to fade by sixty decibels**.

questions.q: Resonances in the Mediterranean tombs fell within the lower register of the adult male ______.
questions.evidence: within the lower register of the adult male voice
questions.explanation: The frequencies fall within the lower register of the **adult male voice**.

questions.q: Conservation plans now often include acoustic measurements taken before any ______ begins.
questions.evidence: taken before any restoration work begins
questions.explanation: Measurements are taken **before any restoration work begins**, because new flooring or lighting can change a chamber's sound.
